questions.q: State the definition of the complement of a set \(A\) with respect to a universal set \(U\) using set-builder notation.
questions.a: The complement of \(A\) is \(A' = \{x \mid x \in U \text{ and } x \notin A\}\). A wrong answer (e.g., \(A' = \{x \mid x \notin A\}\) without mentioning \(U\)) reveals that the student thinks complement is absolute, not relative to a universal set — a fundamental misconception that leads to errors when the universal set changes.

questions.q: Give the correct order of steps to check a student's claim that the complement of a union equals the union of complements.
questions.a: The check runs: (1) Compute the union of the two sets inside the universal set (2) Complement that union by listing what the union misses (3) Compute each set's complement separately and intersect them (4) Compare the two results and correct the conclusion to De Morgan's law with an intersection. A wrong answer that keeps the union on the right shows the student has swapped the two De Morgan identities from memory.

questions.q: Create a real-life problem (in an Indian school context) where finding the complement of a set is necessary to answer the question. Define \(U\), \(A\), and the question clearly.
questions.a: Example: In a school of 500 students (\(U\)), 320 students opted for Mathematics (\(A\)). The principal wants to know how many students did NOT opt for Mathematics to plan alternative classes. The answer is \(n(A') = n(U) - n(A) = 180\). A poor answer would omit the universal set or ask a question that doesn't require complement (e.g., "how many opted for Mathematics?"). This tests whether the student can recognise a complement situation in context.
